description: We are a multidisciplinary team combining NASA MODIS data, statistics, and software development to build an innovative ocean-monitoring application. We are looking for motivated participants with skills in web/mobile development, data visualization, and UI/UX design. If you enjoy technology, Earth observation, data science, and solving real-world environmental problems, you are welcome to join us!
summary: OceanScope is a reproducible trend-detection tool for the Strait of Gibraltar. Using NASA MODIS-Aqua monthly sea surface temperature (SST) and chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) from 2003 to 2023, we ask: is this gateway between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean changing? We analysed spring (Mar-May) and autumn (Sep-Nov) separately with Mann-Kendall tests, Sen's slope, Seasonal Kendall, autocorrelation-robust checks and multiple-testing correction. Spring shows a warming of about +0.033 °C/yr and a Chl-a decline of about -0.029 mg/m3/yr, with the Chl-a decline remaining significant after strict correction; autumn shows no trend. SST and Chl-a are negatively correlated, but in spring this link disappears once the shared trend is removed. Our R analysis confirmed the descriptive statistics and added distribution fitting and copula-based projections with CMIP6 scenarios. Results are delivered as an executed notebook and an interactive Streamlit dashboard. This addresses the challenge "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" by turning satellite time series into clear, honest evidence of ocean change.
details:
WHAT IT DOES:

OceanScope analyses 20 years (2003-2023) of NASA MODIS-Aqua monthly regional SST and Chl-a for the Strait of Gibraltar, for spring (MAM, 63 months) and autumn (SON, 61 months). It detects trends, tests whether SST and Chl-a are linked, and fits statistical distributions for future-scenario work.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data validation: duplicates, missing months, value ranges, date consistency. - Trend tests: Mann-Kendall (Hamed-Rao variant if autocorrelated), Sen's slope with 95% CI, OLS with Newey-West errors, per-month tests, Seasonal Kendall (Hirsch-Slack).

- Multiple-testing correction (Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg); ACF/PACF, ADF and KPSS tests.

- Dependence: Pearson, Spearman, Kendall on raw, anomaly and detrended data, with year-block bootstrap.

- R analysis: normality tests, best-fit distributions (Normal, LogNormal, Gamma, Weibull, Gumbel) and copula-based conditional prediction using CMIP6 (CMCC model, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5). KEY RESULTS - Spring SST +0.033 °C/yr (about +0.66 °C in 21 years); spring Chl-a -0.029 mg/m3/yr. The Seasonal Kendall Chl-a decline stays significant after Holm correction. Autumn: no significant trend in SST or Chl-a. - SST and Chl-a are negatively correlated (Spearman -0.44, n = 124); in spring the link disappears after detrending, so both variables drift together.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Transparent, reproducible evidence of seasonal ocean change in a strategic marine gateway, useful for marine monitoring and as a template for other regions.

TOOLS

Python 3.12 (pandas, numpy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, matplotlib, plotly), Streamlit, Jupyter, R , Excel, Gamma (presentation).

LIMITATIONS

One regional monthly value per month (no maps), two seasons only, units assumed from value ranges (°C, mg/m3), no winter or summer months. Evidence is moderate, not conclusive.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

We prioritised statistical honesty: autocorrelation checks, multiple-testing correction and detrending show which findings are robust and which are not, and an independent R analysis cross-checked our results.
